newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds close flat in lackluster trading.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds close flat in lackluster trading.

text.p: Canadian bonds closed flat in very quiet trade on Monday, with lack of a U.S. market keeping traders sidelined and most investors looking ahead to tomorrow's release of the federal budget, analysts said.

"Nothing has happened. It's extremely quiet and boring. With the U.S. market closed obviously Canadian price movements have been very, very limited," said Andrew Pyle, head of fixed income research with ABN AMRO Bank Canada.
Canada's 30-year bond traded unchanged to yield 6.814 percent. The U.S. 30-year benchmark bond last traded with a yield of 6.53 percent.
The spread between the benchmark bonds remained at 28 basis points.

Analysts said the U.S. President's Day holiday has prompted many Canadian market players to either take a holiday themselves or simply not trade. Analysts said investors are instead focusing their attention on tomorrow's federal budget.

Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin presents budget for fiscal 1997/98 starting April 1 at 1630 EST/2130 GMT. Much like Martin's past budgets, the document is expected to contain conservative spending and interest rate assumptions and present no major surprises to bond investors.

"You would have to stretch the imagination considerably to expect a major surprise from Martin," said ABN's Pyle. Pyle said a budget with conservative assumptions and modest spending initiatives has already been priced into the market.
Analysts said Canadian economic reports out this morning on manufacturing new orders and shipments had no significant effect.
In other prices, the Government of Canada's 7.0 percent bond due 2006 rose C$0.05 to C$106.35 to yield 6.125 percent. The U.S. 10-year bond last traded with a yield of 6.27 percent.
The negative spread between the bonds was 15 basis points.
The three-month cash T-bill traded with a yield of 2.85 percent against the U.S. bill which yielded 5.09 percent.
